Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Greenville-Spartanburg SC
156 PM EST Mon Nov 23 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
Confidence continues to increase for a storm system to impact
the region Wednesday into Thursday with the potential for locally
heavy rain and gusty winds. Confidence in specific rainfall amounts
remains low.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
1. A few showers are possible this afternoon ahead of a cold front.
2. A significant storm system could impact the area Wednesday
into Thursday bringing the potential for locally heavy rain and
frequent wind gusts.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
Key message 1: A few showers are possible this afternoon ahead of
a cold front.

Northwest winds and drying dewpoints over the Cumberland Plateau
of TN/KY indicate a cold front has passed, associated with a
strong continental sfc high centered in the Plains. Though winds
have turned northwest across much of the western Carolinas and
northeast GA, helping to erode the wedge which brought cloud cover
overnight, we have not seen true airmass change and temperatures
will be above normal across the area through evening. Convergence
near the wind shift line is allowing some showers to be generated as
slight SBCAPE is realized. 20-30% PoPs are advertised through late
evening until the instability is exhausted and/or the front settles
past, and cloud cover looks to fill back in for a time tonight into
part of Tuesday. Low temps tonight fall back to near climo in the
mountains but remain above climo in the Piedmont. Showers should
end before temps get cold enough to be worried about a p-type
change in the mountains. Max temps Tuesday will be near climo,
as the high migrates by to our north.


Key message 2: A significant storm system could impact the area
Wednesday into Thursday bringing the potential for locally heavy
rain and frequent wind gusts.

The overall expectation for the midweek period remains the
same--strong cold-air damming setting up by Wednesday, and a period
of widespread rainfall developing late Wednesday and likely lasting
into Thanksgiving morning, in conjunction with a low pressure system
developing near the coast. Since yesterday, however, subtle shifts
in model guidance have caused forecast impacts to trend higher for
the western Carolinas and northeast Georgia. Forecast confidence is
limited due to the sensitivity of the setup to these subtle changes,
as additional slight variation in conditions such as the low track
and the depth of the wedge could cause further significant changes
in impact, one way or the other.

Model consensus still depicts a 1040+ mb sfc high centered over New
England at 12z Wednesday which is expected to foster a classical CAD
event. Easterly flow already should have set up over the wedge by
that time, but amplifies through Wednesday as an upper low/shortwave
over the lower MS Valley induces Miller B-type cyclogenesis near
Florida, tightening the gradient associated with the damming
high and promoting a rapid increase in moisture aloft. The wedge
airmass will be very cold and dry to start, and the onset of
PoPs has been slowed compared to earlier forecast cycles. As a
result the possibility of light wintry precipitation Wednesday has
further decreased over the mountains, with precip most likely not
beginning until after temperatures have warmed above freezing, and
the strong warm nose precluding any possibility of snow. Rainfall
during the day Wednesday is expected to be light, and not likely
of impact beyond wrecking any outdoor holiday plans. Precip would
only reinforce CAD via evaporative cooling, and for that reason
max temps have been adjusted below NBM and closer to raw model
consensus. Most locations northwest of I-85 don't make it out of
the 40s, except the western mountain valleys. With sustained winds
already 10-15 mph in the morning and set to increase, looking like
quite the chilly day.

The thing that stands out as most unusual in guidance late
Wednesday through Thursday morning is the exceptionally strong
easterly LLJ shown on most models on the north side of the low,
with the vast majority of model output suggesting peak 925mb
winds of 50+ kt, and 60-70 kt at 850mb. Curiously the RRFS is a
low outlier in this sense, possibly due to it still depicting the
low tracking offshore. A strong but relatively shallow inversion
associated with the CAD wedge should limit mixing, but even under
the inversion winds are stout enough that 30-40 mph peak gusts
appear a fairly good bet across the CWA late Wednesday through
Thursday morning. Portable outdoor structures such as tents and
holiday decorations may need to be taken in or secured particularly
strongly to withstand such gusts. There does remain potential for
stronger gusts over 40 mph, and if/where those occur, the scale
of power outages most likely would increase. Higher mountain
elevations will be subject to higher gusts, though as usual in a
warm advection regime there is likely to be an even more pronounced
elevation dependency than usual, so winds/gusts at ridgetops may
be considerably greater than readings even 1000 feet below.

As the LLJ ramps up over the course of Wednesday, PWATs go from
roughly daily normal values at daybreak to near 200% of normal
by 00z Thu, appearing to peak (along with the LLJ) in the predawn
hours Thursday, then tapering off from south to north during the
Thanksgiving daytime hours. There continues to be some disagreement
among models in how quickly the upper low near the Gulf Coast
coalesces with another low in the Midwest--some members such as
the 23/12z deterministic GFS keep the features distinct. Those
members depicting the coalescence generally depict a band of precip
moving in from the west Wednesday night or early Thursday ahead
of the combined vort lobe, which may prove to be the main source
of precip for the southwest NC mountains and Savannah Valley.

Ensemble QPF probabilities still don't look overly concerning,
but most members take the incipient low on a more inland track
than on earlier guidance. Even though the low still looks to track
east of the CWA, upslope enhancement into the east-facing Blue
Ridge Escarpment appears more likely, and a pronounced increase in
probabilities of 1" and 2" is noted in that area. A frontogenetic
band of enhanced QPF also still is possible just west of the low
track, but confidence on that aspect is low due to the uncertainty
in the track. A reasonable high-end storm total forecast amount at
this point looks to be 3" to 4" along the east-facing Escarpment,
and 2" to 3" for the eastern Upstate and NC Piedmont. Potential
for high amounts is lower west of the Escarpment and in the western
Upstate and GA. There is still not much of a signal for higher QPF
thresholds to be exceeded and suggest a significant flood risk (3"
in 6 hours, for example) but as higher resolution models begin to
encompass the event over the next 12-24 hours, we should have a
better handle on that possibility.

As westerly winds promote wedge erosion Thursday, max temps warm
back to near normal in the Piedmont and perhaps just below normal
in the mountains. Though the potential for 30+ mph wind gusts
decreases during the day, gusts of 20-30 mph remain possible so
any precautions taken to anchor items Wednesday probably will need
to remain through Thursday as well. Precip wrapping around the
back side of the upper low and upslope NW winds may allow showers
to continue along the NC/TN border through Friday, and a change
from rain to light snow or rime ice still appears possible, with
light accumulations of less than 2 inches not out of the question
there. Gusts in the upslope areas may remain 25-35 mph through
Friday morning, perhaps closer to 40 mph in very high elevations.

Low-impact weather expected for the weekend with daily max temps
rising slightly above normal.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z MONDAY THROUGH SATURDAY/...
At KCLT and elsewhere: Mostly VFR conditions over the TAF sites,
with only lingering MVFR stratocu near KAND, which should lift
and continue scattering through the afternoon. Winds vary at the
terminals, but should gradually increase through the afternoon and
evening hours, while favoring a northerly component. KAVL should
remain northwesterly through much of the forecast period, with
some hint of an downvalley component developing Tuesday afternoon,
just beyond the TAF period. Low-VFR cloud deck will spread over
the the Upstate sites later tonight and remain SCT to BKN through
the period, with lesser extent of cloud cover over the NC TAF
sites by Tuesday morning. Low-end gusts are expected to move into
the area late tonight and linger through at least Friday morning,
while KAVL picks up low-end gusts later this afternoon and remains
in place through much of the TAF period.

Outlook: A low pressure system tracks across the terminals Wednesday
into Thursday bringing widespread rain, associated restrictions,
and gusty winds. Drier and VFR conditions return Thursday night
into Friday but gusty winds will continue.
